title: Allergen menu labeling for restaurants
seoTitle: Allergen menu labeling for restaurants | ROAL
description: Get the basics of allergen menu labeling for restaurants, plus phone scripts, menu updates, and clear ways to handle allergen questions.
question: How should I handle allergen menu labeling on my restaurant menu?
answer: Use clear allergen menu labeling for your menu items, and keep the labels easy to spot and easy to update. For allergy-sensitive questions, make sure your phone host sends the caller to staff with the item, ingredients, and any notes, because menus can’t cover every allergy situation.
summary: You’ll know how to label allergens, train staff, and handle allergy questions by phone without slowing service down.
intro:
Allergen menu labeling should be clear, simple, and easy to update. Put the big allergens right on the menu where callers can see them, and have staff handle any allergy-sensitive question that needs judgment.

That matters because callers often want a fast answer, but allergies are not the place to guess. If your menu, phone script, and kitchen notes all match, you cut confusion for pickup, delivery, and phone orders.

sections.h2: What should allergen menu labeling actually show?
sections.body:
For most independent restaurants, allergen menu labeling should do one job: help a caller spot likely risks before they order. Keep it direct. Use a short note next to the item, such as **contains dairy**, **contains nuts**, or **contains wheat**.

A practical setup for a pizza shop, deli, or family restaurant looks like this:
- Put allergen notes next to each item on the main menu.
- Use the same wording everywhere: website, PDF, photos, and printed menu.
- Keep the labels short enough that a caller can read them fast.
- If a menu item can be changed, note the base recipe first, then modifiers.

Example:
- Pepperoni slice — contains dairy, wheat
- Garden salad — may contain egg in dressing
- Chicken wrap — contains wheat; ask about dressing

If you need a deeper phone menu structure, pair this with [making your menu easy to order by phone](/blog/restaurant-menu-for-phone-orders). That helps callers hear the item first and ask follow-up questions only when needed.

sections.h2: How do I write menu labels that help callers without cluttering the page?
sections.body:
Keep the labels short and predictable. A busy owner does not need a legal essay on every line. A caller needs to know the main allergen risk and who to ask if they need more detail.

Try this simple format:

| Menu item | Label style | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Pizza | Main allergens | contains dairy, wheat |
| Sandwich | Allergen note + sauce note | contains wheat; ask about mayo |
| Soup | Variable items | ask about daily soup ingredients |
| Dessert | Common allergens | contains dairy, egg, nuts |

A few writing rules help:
1. Label the base item, not just the special request.
2. Use “contains” for ingredients you know are in the recipe.
3. Use “may contain” only when that is truly the case for your kitchen flow.
4. If the item changes daily, say so plainly.

For example, a cashier can say: “The chicken parm hero contains dairy and wheat. If you have an allergy, I can have the kitchen check the prep notes before we confirm it.” That is clearer than trying to improvise after the order is already in motion.

sections.h2: How should my phone staff or phone host handle allergy questions?
sections.body:
The safest move is to treat allergy questions as a staff handoff, not a guess. ROAL does this by sending allergy-sensitive questions to staff with a summary, while still collecting the rest of the order details.

A good phone flow is:
1. Take the order items, sizes, modifiers, and notes.
2. Capture the caller’s name and phone.
3. Flag the allergy question for staff review.
4. Confirm the order back only after the kitchen has the needed detail.

Use a script like:
“Thanks for letting me know. I’m sending this to the restaurant team with your allergy note so they can check the ingredients before confirming.”

That is especially useful for combinations like:
- Gluten allergy plus a sauce question
- Nut allergy plus dessert or salad dressing
- Dairy allergy plus cheese, butter, or cream sauces

ROAL also answers menu, hours, address, and parking questions from the restaurant’s public information, but allergy-sensitive calls go to staff. That keeps the phone moving without forcing a bad guess.

sections.h2: How do I keep allergen labels consistent across my menu, website, and PDFs?
sections.body:
Consistency matters more than fancy wording. If your website says one thing, your PDF says another, and your front counter menu says a third thing, callers lose trust fast.

Use one source of truth and update it everywhere at the same time. A simple workflow is:
- Edit the item name and allergen note in one master menu.
- Check the website menu page.
- Check any PDF menu.
- Check menu photos or social posts if customers rely on them.
- Test the wording by reading it out loud.

Worked example:
Say your chicken wrap used to be listed as plain chicken and now includes a garlic sauce with dairy.
- Old label: chicken wrap
- Updated label: chicken wrap — contains wheat, dairy
- Phone note: ask if caller wants sauce on the side

If your menu changes often, this pairs well with [keeping your online menu accurate](/blog/online-menu-accuracy-restaurant). ROAL can read menu details from public pages or from a menu you upload, so the cleaner your source is, the cleaner the phone experience becomes.

sections.h2: What should I tell my team so allergy calls are handled the same way every time?
sections.body:
Give your team one short rule: do not speculate. If a caller asks about an allergen, staff should either verify ingredients or hand the call off to someone who can.

A simple checklist for the counter, kitchen, and phone:
- Know which items have the most common allergens.
- Know which sauces, dressings, and breads need extra checking.
- Never promise a safe result without checking the recipe and prep notes.
- Keep the allergy note visible on the ticket.
- If the caller sounds unsure, ask a follow-up question before confirming.

Here is a useful phrase for staff:
“Let me check the recipe and prep notes before we confirm that item for you.”

For owners who use phone ordering, this is where ROAL helps reduce mistakes. It can take the order and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen, but it will hand off allergy-sensitive questions to staff instead of guessing. That is the right line to draw.

sections.h2: How do allergen labels affect order flow, timing, and costs?
sections.body:
Allergen labeling can actually save time when it is done well, because the caller gets the key facts up front. It can also slow things down if your menu is vague and every order turns into a long back-and-forth.

A simple way to think about it is to compare two paths:

| Scenario | What happens | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Clear labels | Caller spots the issue early | Faster ordering, fewer callbacks |
| Vague labels | Staff has to check every detail | More hold time and more confusion |

If you want a rough cost view, plug in your own numbers:
- Say you lose 5 phone orders a week because callers can’t get clear ingredient answers.
- Say your average order is $28.
- That is $140 in weekly order value you may be missing before you even count delivery-app commission or labor.

takeaways: Use short allergen labels like contains dairy, wheat, or nuts.
Keep the same allergen wording across your menu, website, and PDFs.
Send allergy-sensitive questions to staff instead of guessing on the phone.
Train your team to verify ingredients before confirming a risky item.
A clean menu and a clear phone script save time for everyone.

faq.q: What should I put on a menu for allergen labeling?
faq.a: Put the main allergens next to each item in plain language. Short labels like contains dairy, wheat, egg, or nuts are usually easier for callers to read than long explanations. If an item changes often, say so and direct the caller to staff for details.

faq.q: Do I need to list every allergen on every item?
faq.a: No, but you should list the allergens that are known in the recipe or that matter most for your menu. The goal is clarity, not clutter. If you have a daily soup, rotating special, or changing sauce, mark it clearly so callers know to ask.

faq.q: How should staff answer allergy questions on the phone?
faq.a: Staff should not guess. The safest response is to check the recipe and prep notes, then confirm the order only when the ingredient list is clear. A simple line like, “Let me check that before we confirm it,” works well.
